config_name: Inner Being Analysis Programme — configuration seed
authority: researcher le Roux Cilliers; design = plan moonlit-launching-cocke.md (Appendix A/C)
status: IN-PROGRESS — foundational sections only; not yet loadable into a DB (loader + new DB not built)

meta.purpose: The config-level manifest AND the canonical definition of the rule envelope every config item carries. This is the ONE home for the shared envelope: each section file's meta describes only its own nodes and its own kind-specific `spec`, and refers here for `governs` / `kind` / `status` / `validation`. Do not restate these vocabularies in a section file — a second copy is how the same concept ends up defined four ways (the failure reconciliations.json exists to record).
meta.how_to_read: Every configuration item is a RULE with a fixed anatomy (plan A.10): a common envelope (defined below) + a kind-specific `spec` body (defined in that section's meta). The loader validates the envelope against this file and each `spec` against its section's spec-schema.

id.description: Stable unique code for the rule — the identifier the rest of the config and the runtime refer to it by. Dotted, kind-prefixed, never reused or renumbered once issued (e.g. `enum.role`, `dim.116.locus`, `recon.role-enum`).
id.⚠ when_is_mint: MINT = THE FIRST LOAD INTO THE DB, not the first appearance in a seed file. Clarified 2026-07-15 after the second id rename in one session (module.<ordinal>.<name> -> module.<name>; fetch.* -> raw.*). Both were correct: an id that encodes a mutable property, or a process that turns out not to exist, must be fixed BEFORE anything depends on it. Nothing has ever loaded, so nothing depends on these ids yet. Once cfg_version is loaded into a DB and a run pins to it, ids freeze for real — a rename after that is a migration, not an edit. The rule was always about protecting DEPENDENTS, and there are none yet.

governs.description: WHERE the rule is used — the process(es) AND/OR utility(ies) it applies to. A rule may govern more than one, and `all` is permitted for genuinely cross-cutting rules (provenance). This is the second query axis (plan A.11): asking for a process returns its full governing rule-set, which is what a module loads before it runs. NOTE (researcher ruling, 2026-07-15): `governs` does NOT decide tier. A Tier A (IBA-wide) rule is one where THE SAME RULE APPLIES IN ALL SITUATIONS — universality is the criterion — even though in practice it may only be used in some places, which is what `governs` records. So a wide rule legitimately carries a narrow `governs`.

kind.description: WHAT SORT of rule it is. Selects the spec-schema its `spec` is validated against. (No longer 1:1 with a file — the layout is process-primary; see layout v2 §2.2.)

subject.description: WHAT THE RULE IS ABOUT — the thing it constrains, named plainly (`bearer`, `sense`, `role`, `raw-immutability`, `seed-breadth`). From plan A.10's `composition` (subject · condition · value/threshold · scope), which the first envelope draft under-implemented: it collapsed composition into `spec` and dropped `subject` entirely. ADDED 2026-07-15 on the researcher's ruling (b3).
subject.why_it_is_required: It is the ONLY thing that makes 'the same type of rule for the same item must not be duplicated' mechanically checkable. `governs` says which PROCESS loads a rule; `subject` says what the rule is ABOUT. Two principles about `bearer` in two files are a duplication; a principle about `bearer` and a gate enforcing it are not — same subject, different kind, which is correct and expected.
subject.uniqueness_rule: (kind, subject) must be unique across the whole configurator. A second rule of the same kind about the same subject is a duplication — it must CITE the first, not restate it (layout v2 §2.3).
subject.backfill: ⚠ The 120 items authored before this field existed do not carry it. gate.cfgmaint.subject-present reports the backfill.

status.description: The rule's lifecycle state — whether it is the rule in force, a superseded one kept for provenance, or one whose value is contested and not yet decided.

version.description: Bumped on every change to the rule. A run is pinned to the config version it used, so a change is always traceable to the runs before and after it.

authority.description: WHERE IT COMES FROM — the decision or document the rule derives from (the rule's own provenance). A person + date for a researcher ruling, or a document for a written rule.

reference.description: WHERE IT IS FOUND — the doc §/`[current]` pointer where the rule is stated, so any rule can be read back to its source text. Distinct from `authority`: authority is who/what decided it, reference is where to go read it.

intent.description: HOW IT IS USED — what the rule means and why it exists (its semantics). The human-facing explanation; never a restatement of the `spec`.

satisfaction.description: WHEN IT IS TRUE — the pass condition, stated in plain words: what compliant data or a compliant process looks like. `validation` is the machine form of this.

validation.description: HOW IT IS ENFORCED — the check that decides satisfaction.

axis.description: Whether the check is deterministic code or needs the model. This is the [C]/[I] boundary the whole application turns on: [C] is enforced in code and the model can never override it; [I] is the only place the API is used.

check.description: The check to run, named. Currently free text naming the check (e.g. `value-in-domain`, `pair-direction driver->term`). ⚠ becomes a controlled vocabulary of named checks + parameters once the validation engine is built — see meta.open.check-vocabulary.

enum.description: For domain checks: the `enum.*` item id whose spec.values is the permitted domain. Must resolve to an item in enums.json (loader self-validation, plan A.5).

severity.description: What a failure does to the run.

enforcement.description: WHERE the control is enforced. The signalling node required by the researcher's ruling of 2026-07-15: the schema keeps regulating compliance with DB technology (CHECK · FK · NOT NULL · index), but those controls are SUBSERVIENT to the data-definition requirements defined here. A DB constraint is therefore a PROJECTION of a config rule, never a second definition of it — the configurator-maintenance utility reads this field, diffs config against the live schema, and raises the migration a config change requires. A hand-applied schema constraint on a config-governed control is a defect.

spec.description: The kind-specific body — the rule's actual content (an enum's values, a dimension's shape, a gate's check). Its schema is defined in the meta of the section file that houses this kind, and each kind is validated against its own schema.

open.issue: `validation.check` is free text (e.g. 'value-in-domain', 'pair-direction driver->term', 'mandatory-not-absent + self-interpretable'). The same check is already phrased several ways, and compound checks are jammed into one string with '+'.
open.consequence: The validation engine cannot dispatch on free text, and drift between two phrasings of one check is undetectable.
open.resolve_by: A controlled vocabulary of named checks + typed parameters, decided when gates.json is authored (plan A.8 'how a gate's check_spec is stored').

open.issue: Two overlapping vocabularies: `validation.axis` (C|I) and dimension `spec.derivation` (C|I|I-partial|read-only). dim.103/105/107 declare derivation `I-partial`; dim.114/115 declare `read-only`, which is not an axis value at all.
open.consequence: 'How is this value produced' and 'how is this value checked' are different questions being answered with one blurred vocabulary.
open.resolve_by: Separate them explicitly: axis = how CHECKED (C|I); derivation = how PRODUCED (C|I|I-partial|read-only). Document derivation's vocabulary in dimensions.json meta. Researcher to confirm the split.

open.issue: Researcher ruling 2026-07-15: 'enums define the item, its options, and where it is used; HOW IT IS APPLIED is process configuration.' The ruling names a CAUSE — definitional rules conflated with enforcement rules — not merely an enum instance. dimensions.json has the same conflation and worse: every item carries a `validation` block, plus spec.rule (D3 driver-vs-restraint, D5 bearer!=God), spec.default (D117 literal) and spec.genre_note — all of which are 'how it is applied'.
open.consequence: Read consistently, a dimension defines ve_nr/label/shape/pair-endpoints/mandatory/derivation/enum ONLY, and every check on it becomes a gate in the lexical process's validation node: ~18 validation blocks removed, ~18 gates created.
open.recommendation: YES, it extends — leaving dimensions conflated reintroduces the very cause the ruling names. But the blast radius warrants confirming before acting.
open.resolve_by: researcher decision — BLOCKS authoring of process/lexical.json

open.issue: `validation` is a required envelope field, but a definitional item (an enum, post-ruling) has no validation of its own — the check enforcing its domain is a separate gate rule belonging to the field's process.
open.consequence: Every enum item currently carries a validation block it should not have, and the envelope as written forbids removing it.
open.recommendation: Make `validation` required only for ENFORCEMENT kinds (gate; plus whatever survives on dimension per meta.open.definitional-extends) and not-applicable for DEFINITIONAL kinds (enum). Mark each kind definitional-or-enforcement in vocab.kind.

open.issue: The researcher ruled that each IBA utility gets its own json (config maintenance, process run, discovery, etc.). The 11 `util.*` values now in vocab.governs are drawn from plan 3.3.1/3.3.3 but have not been confirmed as THE set.
open.consequence: The utility set decides how many config files exist and how `governs` is populated.
open.resolve_by: researcher confirmation of the list — BLOCKS authoring of the utility files

open.issue: `git` and `filing` were asked for as IBA-wide config files AND exist as utilities — but the 2026-07-15 ruling forbids one rule having two homes ('the entire rule for an entity must be defined in one place').
open.recommendation: They are UTILITY files; the wide layer cites them by id. The git rules ARE the git utility's configuration; the filing rules ARE the filing utility's.

open.issue: Kinds still undefined: `utility` (new, per the 2026-07-15 ruling) and genre routing (cfg_route). NOTE: kind is NO LONGER 1:1 with a file — the layout is now process-primary (layout v2 §2.2), so `kind` selects the SPEC-SCHEMA while the file selects the process or utility. The `section` field on each vocab.kind value is stale for the same reason.
open.resolve_by: Add kinds, and retire vocab.kind's `section` field, as the layout is applied.

open.issue: `lexicon` means two different things: the lexical-decomposition PROCESS (vocab.governs) and the Strong's-gloss raw TABLE. Flagged in the plan (A.11) and still unreconciled.
open.consequence: 'lexicon rules' is ambiguous in exactly the layer that failed validation.
open.resolve_by: Rename one. Candidate: the process becomes `lexical`, the raw table keeps `lexicon`. Researcher decision.

open.issue: The config's own vocabularies (vocab.governs/kind/status/axis/severity) are defined HERE in prose-ish JSON, not as `enum.*` items in enums.json — yet they are word-groups with codes, which is exactly what enums.json is for.
open.consequence: Two homes for 'what is a controlled vocabulary in this system'.
open.resolve_by: Decide whether the config self-hosts (its own vocabularies become enum items, loader bootstraps from them) or whether meta-vocabularies are deliberately held apart as the envelope's own definition. Researcher decision — affects the loader.

open.issue: 49 gates are declared in the configurator; 38 are LIVE. The kernel implements 6. The other 32 LIVE gates have no code. Most legitimately await the validation engine (they check STUDY data that does not exist yet) — but 5 CONFIG gates should run today and do not: gate.cfgmaint.spec-schema, .acyclic, .alias-covers-retired, .no-reconcile-in-scope, and .seed-declared (now implemented in cfg_apply.py).
open.consequence: A gate declared LIVE that nothing runs is worse than no gate: the config asserts the control is in force, and a reader — human or model — has no way to tell it is not. This is the failure record's 'a scan gate silently non-operational across whole books', reproduced in the tool built to prevent it.
options: A: implement them — each is small (spec-schema needs the per-kind schemas; acyclic needs pipeline.json; alias-covers-retired needs a retired-value set; no-reconcile-in-scope needs a run plan)
B: mark them INACTIVE until implemented — honest, and enum.status now HAS that value precisely for 'defined and correct, nothing uses it yet'
C: leave them LIVE (the status quo — the config lies about what it enforces)
open.recommendation: B NOW, A next. INACTIVE is exactly what these are: defined, correct, unwired. Marking them LIVE while nothing runs them is the config asserting a control it does not have — and the researcher's own INACTIVE ruling was made for this precise case. C is how a scan gate goes silently non-operational for months.

vocabularies_moved.authority: researcher ruling 2026-07-15 (a) — no nomenclature without its description in the enums
vocabularies_moved.what: The configurator's own vocabularies (governs · kind · status · axis · enforcement · severity) moved from _manifest.meta.vocabularies into wide/enums.json as enum.* items on 2026-07-15.
vocabularies_moved.why: They are nomenclature like any other. Holding them here was a SECOND HOME for them — forbidden by the same day's ruling (b3), and caught by gate.cfgmaint.nomenclature-has-enum against this very file.
consequences: THE CONFIG SELF-HOSTS — settles meta.open.self-hosting as YES.
ENUM VALUES ARE OBJECTS {value, description} — settles meta.open.value-metadata as option B. A bare string has no description and so cannot be cross-checked.
The envelope now CITES enum ids; it no longer carries vocabularies. The kernel reads them from the register at run time and still knows no vocabulary VALUES.
vocabularies_moved.outstanding: The 11 lexical enums still hold bare-string values and need sourced descriptions — a sourcing job against the live DB, not a typing job. See utility/config-maintenance.json open.cfgmaint.vocab-migration.

layout.shape: Two tiers. TIER A (wide/) = rules where THE SAME RULE APPLIES IN ALL SITUATIONS, plus one file per UTILITY. TIER B (process/) = one file per study process, with facets as NODES (process · entities · output · validation · naming · filing), not as separate files.
layout.note: The file layout is authoring ergonomics, not architecture — at runtime every rule is a row carrying `kind` + `governs`, queryable on both axes regardless of which file authored it. The researcher's observation stands: consolidated into the DB, these plausibly become ONE table (see meta.open.rule-table). Files may therefore be re-cut cheaply; the envelope may not.

last_change.why: CRITICAL: step.connection v1 would have broken the study. .env holds the REMOTE url and UNTAGGED ESV; the client hard-codes localhost + ESV_th and ignores .env. v1 ruled 'rewrite the client to read .env' — which would silently switch the study to remote/untagged with no error. Names from .env, VALUES from the client.

★ how_this_config_is_maintained.the_rule: cfgmaint.sole-write-path — scripts/cfg_apply.py is the ONLY writer. Hand-edits are what it replaces.
★ how_this_config_is_maintained.the_lifecycle: stage -> apply -> VALIDATE -> reject-or-commit. Validation happens BEFORE the live config is touched; an invalid edit never reaches disk.
★ how_this_config_is_maintained.⚠ the_confession: Every change on 2026-07-15 before config_version 0.2.0 was a HAND-EDIT: an ad-hoc script mutated the JSON and the kernel ran afterwards. That is the inverse of cfgmaint.load-lifecycle, and it cost exactly what the rule predicts — invalid config reached disk three times in one session, including a shell-quoting bug that silently emptied enum value descriptions and which the kernel PASSED (a mangled string is still a string). The researcher asked 'are you using the configurator maintenance utility?'. The answer was no. cfg_apply.py exists because of that question.
★ how_this_config_is_maintained.what_still_is_not_enforced: 5 gates are declared LIVE and have no implementation: spec-schema, acyclic, alias-covers-retired, no-reconcile-in-scope, and (until now) seed-declared. A gate declared LIVE with no code is the failure this programme exists to end — 'rules not encoded, dependence on memory' — reproduced inside the configurator. Tracked as meta.open.gates-declared-not-implemented.
★ how_this_config_is_maintained.the_commit_bug_20260715: cfg_apply.py v1 COPIED staging over live instead of MIRRORING it, so a file DELETED in staging survived in live. The fetch->raw merge validated clean in staging (fetch.json gone) and produced an INVALID live config (fetch.json alive, 18 duplicate ids). THE TOOL VALIDATED ONE STATE AND WROTE ANOTHER — the exact failure class it was built to prevent, in its second run. Fixed: commit now removes live files absent from staging. The lesson is the one the whole programme keeps relearning: a control is not what you intended, it is what the code does.
